subject: mathematics
question_text: Find the domain of the real valued function f(x) = √(x² − 1) + 1/√(x² − 3x + 2).

mark_split.label: Conditions for the function to be defined

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IA (2026-27 edition), book p.12, chapter 2 FUNCTIONS, Very Short Answer question 19 part (a-ii). Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. ⚠ THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the Mathematics-IA volume prints no per-step mark allocation on any answer. recall_prompt: Say how you would find this domain — the conditions the formula forces, and the answer.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Write both conditions
steps.margin_note: One of the two marks is for the conditions alone. Write every one of them down before solving any.
steps.memory_tip: Two terms, two conditions: ≥ 0 for the plain root, > 0 for the root under a fraction.
lines: The second root is in a denominator, so

recall.must_convey: That the first root needs x² − 1 ≥ 0 while the second, being in a denominator, needs x² − 3x + 2 strictly greater than zero.
accept: first root at least zero and the second strictly positive because it is in the denominator
x squared minus one greater than or equal to zero and x squared minus three x plus two greater than zero
the second one cannot be zero since we divide by it so strictly positive
second root denominator lo undi so zero avvakoodadu strictly positive undali
two conditions one with equals allowed and one without
heard_as: x squared minus three x plus two

steps.why: Each term must be defined on its own. The only difference between the two roots is that the second sits in a denominator, and that is what turns ≥ 0 into > 0 and removes x = 1 and x = 2.
common_mistakes: Using ≥ 0 for the second condition, which wrongly keeps x = 1 and x = 2 where the denominator is zero.
Writing only one condition and ignoring the other term.

steps.label: Intersect the two sets
steps.margin_note: The second mark is the interval itself. Write it in interval form, and check every bracket.
steps.memory_tip: Both terms must work at the same x, so take the overlap of (1) and (2). Never their union.
lines: The domain is the intersection of (1) and (2).
The other two overlaps are empty.

recall.must_convey: That the answer is the intersection of the two sets, giving minus infinity to minus one closed, union two to infinity open.
accept: intersect the two sets to get minus infinity to minus one union two to infinity
take the common part of both conditions not the union
x at most minus one or x greater than two strictly
rendu conditions common part theesukovali union kaadu
closed at minus one and open at two
heard_as: x squared minus three x plus two

steps.why: A sum of two terms is defined only where both terms are defined, so the answer is the overlap of the two sets, not everything either one allows on its own.
common_mistakes: Taking the union of the two sets, which lets in values where one term is undefined.
Including [1, 2], where the second denominator is zero or negative.
